Yields Jump as Inflation Comes in Hotter Than Expected
 
Plus, stocks fall as the case for interest-rate hikes grows
 
By Heard on the Street Staff
 
 
KEN CEDENO/REUTERS
 

This is an edition of the Markets P.M. newsletter, a recap of the day’s most important markets moves, delivered after the closing bell. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

What Happened in Markets Today

 

Bond yields rose sharply after inflation in October overshot expectations. Consumer prices rose 0.4% from the previous month, compared with economists’ expectations of a 0.3% increase; core inflation, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, was also hotter than expected. The 10-year Treasury benchmark briefly touched 5%.

 

The data could strengthen the case for Fed interest-rate hikes. Fed governor Christopher Waller and Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan both gave hawkish comments today suggesting that the central bank might consider raising rates faster. After the inflation report, traders moved to price in a roughly 10% chance of a half-percentage point increase next month.

 

Stocks traded lower, led by the Nasdaq composite, which was down 0.7% at the close. Shares of Nvidia, which has found itself at the center of a spy scandal, extended yesterday’s losses, falling nearly 5%.

 

Anthropic will seek a valuation of around $1.3 trillion in its initial public offering. Anthropic is meeting with prospective investors this week and shares are expected to start trading Thursday of next week. Anthropic’s IPO is seen as a litmus test for markets on edge over the AI trade. Its targeted valuation is far below the roughly $2 trillion figure that had been floated months ago.

One Big Story

 
 
ANTHONY WALLACE/AGENCE FRANCE-PRESSE/GETTY IMAGES
 

In June 2024, Nvidia Chief Executive Jensen Huang was in Taipei for an annual computer-industry trade show. Late one night, a group of technology executives gathered at a bar. Among them was Alice Huang, then a top leader at a Singapore-based data center company.

 

Huang said she could likely persuade the Nvidia chief to join them. “Jensen’s a great friend of mine,” she said to the group, according to a tech executive who was present. She sent a text, and a few minutes later, Jensen Huang arrived and ordered a whiskey. He held forth briefly to the gathered executives, then left alone, saying he was tired, the person said.
